title: Can China Turn Its Small Modular Reactor Ambitions into Commercial Reality?
gist: China can build first-of-a-kind SMRs (Linglong One, 125 MWe, due online end-2026) but they cost far more than large reactors and its grid, surplus power and subsidized large-reactor fleet crowd out use cases, so domestic SMR commercialization looks niche (industrial heat, district heating) rather than a mass market.

themes.theme: SMR cost gap vs large reactors

insights.claim: Chinese experts estimate small modular reactor electricity is roughly 20 percent more expensive (levelized cost) than power from conventional large reactors because of lost economies of scale.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: SMR cost curves are not yet competitive; avoid pricing in solar/EV-style cost collapse for Chinese SMRs near term.
insights.locator: From Demonstration to Market Commodity?

insights.claim: Linglong One is reportedly up to twice as expensive to build per kilowatt as an average large pressurized-water reactor and its electricity costs 50 percent more, and the project has suffered delays that could raise costs further.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Even China's flagship SMR is a showpiece economically; read-through is negative for near-term SMR unit economics globally.
insights.locator: Linglong One, currently China's most prominent SMR project

insights.claim: The Shandong high-temperature gas-cooled reactor demonstration suffered construction overruns and a reduction in nominal capacity, with construction cost per kilowatt assessed at more than twice that of a Hualong One large reactor.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Advanced-design SMRs carry first-of-a-kind overrun risk; watch capex disclosures for follow-on units.
insights.locator: high-temperature gas-cooled reactor project in Shandong Province

insights.claim: Reducing construction time and unit cost to win repeat orders, via simplification, standardization, factory fabrication and faster on-site assembly, is the only viable path to a real SMR market, and progress so far is elusive.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Track order repetition and build times for second units as the real signal of SMR commercial viability.
insights.locator: Chinese experts recognize that to make SMRs genuinely modular

insights.claim: Beijing has not made SMRs a policy priority: state-backed financing already subsidizes large reactors, squeezing out SMR cost advantages, and support is limited to technology development and demonstration.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Do not expect a Chinese state-driven SMR build-out comparable to its large-reactor fleet; subsidy announcements would be the trigger to revisit.
insights.locator: The absence of substantial targeted support so far

insights.claim: China is gradually trimming preferential tax treatment for nuclear: a late-2025 policy eliminated VAT refunds for newly approved reactors and phases them out for approved projects, which weakens SMR economics absent SMR-specific incentives.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Removal of tax support is a headwind for Chinese nuclear project returns, especially for costlier SMRs.
insights.locator: Instead, Beijing has been gradually reducing preferential tax treatment

insights.claim: Possible revenue levers for Chinese SMRs include reclassifying nuclear as renewable for the Green Electricity Certificate system or making SMRs eligible for the CCER carbon-offset system, but CCER has no methodology for SMR emission reductions.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: A CCER methodology for SMRs or green-certificate eligibility would be a concrete positive catalyst to watch.
insights.locator: On the energy regulatory side

insights.claim: Unlike in the US, where big tech backs SMRs to power data centers, China shows no comparable AI-energy pull for SMRs because it is adding coal, renewables and conventional nuclear faster than demand, producing regional surpluses and curtailment.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: The AI-power-for-nuclear thesis is US-specific; Chinese SMR names should not be valued on a data-center demand story.
insights.locator: What Market?

insights.claim: China's interconnected grid with ultra-high-voltage transmission removes the standard SMR use case of powering remote unconnected areas and favors large plants that capture economies of scale.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Grid strength is a structural reason Chinese SMR demand is limited.
insights.locator: China's highly developed and interconnected power grid

insights.claim: A key paradox: the indigenized technology and supply chains of China's large nuclear fleet enabled rapid SMR development, yet the success of the large-plant build-out has crowded out SMR use cases; the remaining hinterlands face cheap renewables and data centers sited there under Eastern Data, Western Compute.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: The best-case domestic niche is industrial, not grid-scale baseload.
insights.locator: Herein lies a key paradox for SMRs

insights.claim: The most promising domestic SMR markets are industrial parks and district heating, where combined electricity, heat, steam, hydrogen or desalinated water suits a few-hundred-MW reactor better than a gigawatt-scale one; the Shandong HTGR produces hotter steam than conventional PWRs.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Watch chemical-complex and industrial-park nuclear-heat pilots as the realistic SMR demand pocket.
insights.locator: SMRs' Optimal Use Cases

insights.claim: China's 2025 radiation rules dropped the blanket 10 km siting distance from cities of 100,000+ and cut the minimum planning-restricted-area for SMRs from 5 km to 1 km, enabling deployment nearer industrial users.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Relaxed siting is a necessary enabler for the industrial-heat SMR case.
insights.locator: Regulatory Uncertainty

insights.claim: Regulatory guidance lags: nuclear sites and chemical plants fall under different rules and authorities, and the National Nuclear Safety Administration issued only high-level Technical Opinions on SMR safety in August 2026 without detailed licensing standards.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Absence of executable licensing rules is a major brake on investment; detailed standards would be a positive signal.
insights.locator: Regulatory guidance, however, still lags

insights.claim: A regulatory dilemma applies: uncertainty discourages investment, but regulators cannot move further without empirical evidence from construction and deployment of immature SMR technologies.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Progress will be incremental and tied to demonstration results.
insights.locator: Even within the nuclear sector, the lack of clear

themes.theme: Fuel, spent fuel and public acceptance

insights.claim: Uranium supply is unlikely to constrain Chinese nuclear through the 2040s despite heavy import dependence, given a mix of domestic production, stockpiling, Chinese control of overseas mines and market purchases.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: The SMR bottleneck is fuel form, not natural uranium; uranium-supply fears for China are overstated.
insights.locator: Constrained Supply Chain

insights.claim: Many advanced SMR designs need HALEU enriched to 5-20 percent versus under 5 percent for traditional light-water fuel; China makes HALEU for its HTGRs but faces significant hurdles scaling other HALEU fuel forms.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: HALEU capacity is a gating item for advanced SMR deployment in China, as elsewhere.
insights.locator: The challenge will be to meet fuel needs for advanced non-light-water reactor designs

insights.claim: China's capabilities to reprocess spent fuel from several advanced non-light-water reactor types remain technologically immature, despite the 2025 Atomic Energy Law reaffirming a closed fuel cycle.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Back-end fuel management is an under-appreciated constraint on diversified SMR fleets.
insights.locator: China will similarly face challenges in managing used fuels

insights.claim: Dispersed standalone SMRs face security cost and local-opposition problems: replicating large-plant security at every site may be uneconomic, siting near residents hurts acceptance, and past organized opposition has delayed or cancelled Chinese nuclear projects.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Public acceptance can limit where proximity-sited SMRs are built, even in an authoritarian system.
insights.locator: Chinese NIMBYism

insights.claim: Roughly half the world's reactors under construction are in China, which expects to surpass the US in installed nuclear capacity by 2030; Linglong One (125 MWe, Hainan) would be the world's first commercial land-based small modular PWR if it starts by end-2026.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: China dominates large-reactor build-out; the Linglong One start-up is a near-term milestone to monitor.
insights.locator: If it begins operation as expected by the end of 2026

insights.claim: Chinese analysts expect the first global wave of SMR deployment around 2030, contingent on manufacturing capacity and bending the cost curve down as China did with solar, EVs and batteries; the author expects the overseas market for Chinese SMRs to stay limited for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Export upside for Chinese SMRs should be discounted; commercialization is a post-2030 story.
insights.locator: Chinese analysts expect the first wave of SMR deployment globally

insights.claim: Volume is needed for modularization cost reductions and a large addressable market is needed for volume, so China's domestic SMR case will likely stay selective and niche (industrial heat, steam, district heating, desalination, off-grid power) and advance incrementally.
insights.speaker: Tong Zhao
insights.so_what: Expect slow, experimental SMR roll-out rather than a step-change in Chinese nuclear capacity growth from SMRs.
insights.quote: the potential of China’s SMR industry doesn’t match the reality
insights.locator: Conclusion
